AI is rapidly rewriting the process and paperwork layer for Sheet Metal Workers, but on-site judgment and professional experience still rest with people. This article breaks down the specific impact and how to respond.
It does not suit people who dislike noise and dust, cannot stay focused, or lack dimensional sense. Sheet metal shops are loud and smell of metal; dimensional errors create scrap.

A common path is technical school or apprenticeship, learning drawings, measurement, marking, and cutting, starting as a shear and brake assistant, practicing hand forming, learning CNC bending and laser programming, and advancing to technician, crew leader, or shop technical lead.
This career suits hands-on, resilient people with spatial awareness. If you read drawings, calculate flat-pattern dimensions, and accept workshop hammering, it can be a good fit.

Sheet metal workers mark, cut, bend, form, join, and install sheet metal from drawings to produce ducts, enclosures, and structural parts. They are a key skilled trade in building ventilation, metal products, and equipment manufacturing.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 127,000 sheet metal workers were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to rise to 130,100 by 2034, a net increase of about 3,100 jobs, with about 10,600 openings annually. The median annual wage in 2026 is approximately $60,800 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI and automation will not immediately replace sheet metal workers, but they will change the work. Laser cutting, CNC bending, and nesting software are taking over cutting and standard bending, shifting workers from manual calculation and cutting toward programming, setup, hand finishing, and field installation. Complex layout, welding skill, and on-site adjustment remain irreplaceable.
